rss.title: Measuring how AI agents handle everyday wet-lab science
rss.summary: OpenAI introduces BioBasicsBench, a 100-task benchmark measuring how well AI agents interpret raw experimental data and handle everyday wet-lab science.
rss.text_excerpt:
Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. As part of that mission, we want to help scientists accelerate biological research—from understanding disease to developing new treatments. For AI agents to contribute, they need to reliably interpret the experimental evidence scientists work with every day in wet labs, where they run experiments with biological samples. Everyday wet-lab work involves failed experiments, ambiguous images and conflicting observations. Existing benchmarks are built around charts and images selected for scientific papers may miss this ambiguity and the troubleshooting it requires. That’s why we’re introducing BioBasicsBench, a new benchmark developed with Ligo, a biotech company focused on enzyme design, to measure how well agents handle routine wet-lab analysis. The benchmark’s 100 tasks test whether agents can interpret raw experimental data, identify errors, and recognize when the evidence cannot support a conclusion. Getting these tasks right matters because misreading an image or overlooking a problem with the controls used to check an experiment’s results can lead scientists to draw the wrong conclusion and spend time on experiments that won’t help answer their question. At the ‘xhigh’ setting, which allows more reasoning per task, GPT‑6 Astra earned an average of 66.7% of the available credit, compared with 43.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. The results show progress on routine lab analysis, with room for further improvements in interpreting images, checking controls and applying experimental context. BioBasicsBench uses raw experimental evidence, from gel images and colony plates to microscopy and instrument readouts. BioBasicsBench has 100 tasks across five areas of routine wet-lab work: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Tasks range from simple requests, such as reading the molecular weight of a DNA sample in a gel, to detailed assay analysis, but all involve routine work that wet-lab scientists should be able to complete reliably. Scientists created the tasks using data from their own experiments, pairing each question with expert-written grading criteria. rss.title: A thousand fewer paths to root
rss.summary: OpenAI built an autonomous pipeline that found, validated, and generated patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel.
rss.text_excerpt:
Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area. Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access. We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches. In June, as part of our Patch the Planet initiative , we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches. Summary At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results. The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes. In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. # PDD ## What PDD is In PDD, you write prompts and Stories. The prompts are the source of your program. The PDD interpreter runs the prompts with an AI that acts as the code, so you can check and try the program before any code exists. Then your agent writes the code from the approved prompts. ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Prompt
the source"] --> S["Story
what a user can do"] S --> C["Test
pdd test"] C --> T["Simulate
pdd simulate"] T --> A["Approve
pdd approve"] A --> K["Code
from the prompts"] ``` PDD is the `pdd` command and a set of skills for your agent. Your agent writes the prompts, the Stories, the tests and the code. The PDD interpreter runs the checks and the simulation. Only you approve. ## Install You need [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 22.20 or newer, [Git](https://git-scm.com), and the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com) signed in with `gh auth login`. You also need an agent that can use skills, and access to the PDD interpreter (see [Access](#access)). PDD is tested on macOS and Linux. ```sh npm install -g github:promptdriven/pdd npx skills add promptdriven/pdd -g pdd --version cd your-repo pdd setup ``` 1. `npm install -g github:promptdriven/pdd` installs the `pdd` command. 2. `npx skills add promptdriven/pdd -g` adds the PDD skills for your agents. The installer finds the agents on your computer, or asks you which agents get the skills. It can say `Failed to install` for an agent that cannot have global skills. That agent still gets them. 3. `pdd --version` must print `0.1.20`. Then every agent chat in the repo knows that the project uses PDD. A second run changes nothing. To update, run the 2 install commands and `pdd setup` again, then start a new agent chat. [![Go Version](https://img.shields.io/badge/Go-1.25+-00ADD8?style=for-the-badge&logo=go&labelColor=1a1b26)](https://go.dev) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-9ece6a?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=1a1b26)](LICENSE) [![Platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/Platform-macOS%20%7C%20Linux-7aa2f7?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=1a1b26)](https://github.com/colonyops/hive) [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/colonyops/hive?style=for-the-badge&color=e0af68&labelColor=1a1b26)](https://github.com/colonyops/hive/releases) [Documentation](https://hivedesktop.com/cli/) | [Getting Started](https://hivedesktop.com/cli/getting-started/) | [Configuration](https://hivedesktop.com/cli/configuration/) | [Contributing](#contributing)
--- This repository holds two programs on one session engine: - **hive**, the CLI/TUI documented below (`cmd/hive`). - **Hive Desktop**, a desktop app with an inbox that collects pull requests, issues, and alerts into feeds, a Code area for the same sessions, and agent chat workspaces (`cmd/desktop`). Download it and read its docs at [hivedesktop.com](https://hivedesktop.com/desktop/getting-started/). ## Installation ```bash brew install tmux brew install colonyops/tap/hive ``` Or install directly with Go: ```bash go install github.com/colonyops/hive@latest ``` Pre-built binaries are also available on the [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/colonyops/hive/releases) page. ## Overview Hive manages isolated git sessions for running AI agents in parallel. Instead of manually managing git worktrees or directories, hive handles cloning, recycling, and spawning terminal sessions with your preferred AI tool (Claude, Aider, Codex). Each hive session is a complete git clone in a dedicated directory with its own terminal environment. # dachshund ### All your agents. One memory. **Claude Code remembers one decision. Codex remembers another. Cursor remembers the exception.**
dachshund finds the memory files your agents already keep, brings them into one Markdown library, and serves that library back through MCP. No account, no cloud, no model requirement. [![Download for macOS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Download-macOS%20Apple%20Silicon-111111?logo=apple&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Ewen2015/dachshund/releases/download/v0.1.26/dachshund-0.1.26-arm64.dmg) [![Status](https://img.shields.io/badge/status-working%20MVP-111111)](docs/MVP.md) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-111111)](LICENSE) [![Local](https://img.shields.io/badge/runtime-local%20only-25845f)](#privacy) **[English](README.md)** · **[简体中文](README.zh-CN.md)** **[Download](#download)** · **[First run](#first-run)** · **[Supported agents](#supported-agents)** · **[How it works](#how-it-works)** · **[Docs](#documentation)** · **[Research](research/cross-agent-memory-products.md)**

## Is dachshund for you? Every agent keeps its own partial model of you. A project rule lives in Claude Code. A failed approach lives in Codex. A typography preference lives in Cursor. Switching tools means losing context or repeating yourself. dachshund takes the memory that already exists and puts it behind one quiet surface: - **Discover what is already on your Mac.** Read known agent memory locations without rewriting the originals. - **See how each agent remembers.** Open an agent to compare its native memory model with dachshund's shared taxonomy, with an expandable mechanism diagram. - **Keep one portable library.** Store the unified result as plain Markdown, with source provenance retained. - **See cross-agent echoes.** When two agents remember the same thing, keep one memory and show every source. - **Share forward.** Promote a source memory into a durable dachshund copy, or write through MCP with the calling agent retained as provenance. - **Keep the library current.** Sync on demand or rescan [TRUNCATED]
